beats.text: Ecology of Predation asks when useful dependence becomes difficult to escape.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: It follows resource capture from biological interactions into institutions and artificial intelligence.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: The comparison is a bounded hypothesis, not a moral law borrowed from nature.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Its distinctive question is whether a relationship preserves another party’s ability to refuse and learn.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Readers can examine the conditions separating mutual benefit from increasingly one-sided dependence.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: A useful personal agent can accumulate memory that makes its owner increasingly dependent.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Changing providers may require more than exporting a collection of files.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: The book asks whether learned functions, relationships, and active permissions can move too.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: That is a specific mechanism through which convenience could make exit costly.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: The example earns its biological comparison only when the resource, cost, and adaptation remain identifiable.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: The wider argument compares capture, counter-adaptation, cooperation, and the distribution of learning speed.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Biological patterns supply questions without deciding what human institutions should permit.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: The proposed alternative protects understanding, refusal, apprenticeship, and meaningful changes of partner.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Its forecasts remain claims that future evidence could contradict.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: This makes the book a framework to examine, rather than a universal explanation of conflict.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Begin with the epistemic note, which states when the central analogy is legitimate.
